passages.title: Barriers, rotation and trap crops — control without spraying — Floating row covers
passages.text:
A lightweight fabric laid over a crop physically excludes flying pests. It is
the single most reliable control against pests that must arrive from outside,
because it does not depend on the pest's behaviour, the weather or the timing of
a spray.

It works only if it is sealed. Edges must be buried or weighted along their whole
length, and any gap is a doorway. It must also go on *before* the pest arrives —
a cover laid over an infestation is a greenhouse for it.

The critical exception is any crop that needs insect pollination. Covers must
come off at flowering, or the crop sets no fruit. For leaf and root crops that
never flower before harvest, they can stay on the whole season.

passages.title: Barriers, rotation and trap crops — control without spraying — Collars, bands and trenches
passages.text:
Cutworms sever seedlings at soil level, and a simple collar — a ring of card or
tin pushed a little into the soil around the stem — stops them physically. It is
laborious and it is close to absolute, which makes it worthwhile for a small
number of high-value transplants.

Sticky bands around stems intercept crawling pests, and steep-sided trenches
trap flightless species migrating on foot. None of these need a product, a
sprayer or a re-entry period.

passages.title: Barriers, rotation and trap crops — control without spraying — Rotation only works against the immobile
passages.text:
Rotation starves soil-dwelling pests with narrow host ranges by removing the
host from the ground they are in. It is genuinely effective against wireworms,
white grubs and other larvae that spend a year or more in the soil and cannot
travel far.

It does almost nothing against strong fliers. Moving a crop to the next field
does not inconvenience a moth. The rule of thumb is that rotation works in
inverse proportion to how far the pest can move — and its effect depends on the
distance between this year's crop and last year's ground, not merely on the
sequence written in a plan.

Rotating after grass or a grassy cover crop is a specific and common trap: those
are exactly the conditions that build up wireworm and grub populations, and the
following crop inherits them.

passages.title: Barriers, rotation and trap crops — control without spraying — Trap crops and the step everyone forgets
passages.text:
A trap crop is a more attractive planting used to draw a pest away from the main
crop — a border of a preferred host, sown early so it is at the stage the pest
wants when the pest arrives.

The step that gets missed is destroying it. A trap crop left standing becomes a
nursery: the pest breeds up in it and moves into the main crop in far greater
numbers than would ever have arrived naturally. It must be destroyed, or
treated, while the pests are still concentrated in it.

passages.title: Beneficial insects — the workforce you already have — The predators worth recognising
passages.text:
Ladybirds are widely known as adults and almost universally destroyed as larvae.
The larva is the more voracious stage and looks nothing like the beetle: a small,
elongated, alligator-shaped, blue-grey creature with orange markings, moving
quickly over leaves. Farmers regularly report it as a pest.

Hoverfly larvae are legless, translucent green or brown maggots that lie among
aphid colonies and are easy to miss entirely; the adults look like small wasps
but hover and do not sting. Lacewing larvae are similar in shape to ladybird
larvae with large curved jaws. Ground beetles are fast, dark, shiny beetles that
run from a lifted stone and eat soil-dwelling larvae and eggs at night.

passages.title: Beneficial insects — the workforce you already have — Parasitic wasps and the mummies they leave
passages.text:
Most parasitic wasps in a crop are tiny — a few millimetres, often barely
visible — and they do not sting people. The female lays an egg inside a pest,
and the larva develops within it.

Their unmistakable sign is the aphid mummy: a swollen, papery, bronze or tan
aphid glued to the leaf, often with a neat round exit hole. A colony full of
mummies is a colony being destroyed without any intervention, and spraying it is
straightforwardly counterproductive. Learning to spot mummies is one of the
highest-value skills in this whole subject.

passages.title: Beneficial insects — the workforce you already have — Why spraying can make an infestation worse
passages.text:
Pest species usually breed faster than the things that eat them. After a
broad-spectrum spray both populations crash, but the pest recovers first, and it
recovers into a field with no predators left. The second peak is often higher
than the one that was sprayed — the standard name for this is pest resurgence.

This is the mechanism behind the observation that a farm which sprays routinely
often has worse pest problems than a neighbour who does not.

passages.title: Beneficial insects — the workforce you already have — Keeping them without buying them
passages.text:
Predators and parasitoids need three things the crop itself rarely provides:
nectar and pollen for the adults, shelter over winter, and alternative prey when
pest numbers are low.

Flowering strips, hedgerows, uncut margins, tolerance of some flowering weeds,
and simply not clearing every scrap of cover in autumn all supply these. Buying
in released predators is expensive and usually temporary; making the farm a
place they stay is neither.

passages.title: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) — the caterpillar-specific bacterium — Why it only affects caterpillars
passages.text:
Bt is a soil bacterium that produces crystal proteins. Those crystals only
become toxic when they are dissolved, and dissolving them requires the strongly
alkaline gut that caterpillars have and most other animals do not. Once
activated, the protein binds to specific receptors in the gut wall, the gut is
perforated, and the caterpillar stops feeding within hours and dies over a day
or two.

The requirement for both an alkaline gut and the matching receptor is why Bt is
so unusually selective. Beetles, aphids, bees, earthworms, birds and humans lack
one or both, which is why Bt is one of the few insecticides that can be used
without wrecking the beneficial insect population in the crop.

Different Bt subspecies target different orders. The one sold for caterpillars
does not work on beetle larvae, and vice versa — buying the wrong subspecies is
a common and completely invisible reason for failure.

passages.title: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) — the caterpillar-specific bacterium — It must be eaten
passages.text:
Bt is a stomach poison with no contact activity at all. A caterpillar that walks
through a treated patch is unharmed; it has to eat treated leaf. Three things
follow from that.

Spray where the caterpillars are feeding, which is often the underside of leaves
or deep in the whorl of a cereal. Spray while they are small, because young
larvae eat proportionally more surface leaf and are far more susceptible. And
accept that any caterpillar already tunnelled inside a stem, a fruit or a rolled
leaf will never encounter the spray — for borers, the window is the short period
after hatching and before entry.

passages.title: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) — the caterpillar-specific bacterium — It does not last
passages.text:
Sunlight breaks Bt down quickly, typically within a day or two of application.
This is good for residues and bad for planning: it means Bt has essentially no
persistence, so it only controls the larvae present when you spray. Eggs that
hatch afterwards are unaffected.

That short life is also why Bt is best matched to a scouting programme. Applied
on a calendar it mostly misses; applied when monitoring shows a hatch, it works
well.

passages.title: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) — the caterpillar-specific bacterium — Stopping feeding comes before dying
passages.text:
Treated caterpillars stop eating almost immediately but can remain visibly alive
for a day or more. Crop damage stops long before the caterpillars disappear, so
judging the result by how many are still moving will consistently understate it.
Always follow the product label and the rules of your certification body.

passages.title: Diatomaceous earth and kaolin clay — the mineral dusts — Diatomaceous earth abrades, so it must stay dry
passages.text:
Diatomaceous earth is the fossilised silica skeletons of microscopic algae.
Under a microscope the particles are sharp; against an insect they abrade the
waxy cuticle, and the insect dies of water loss. There is no poison and nothing
for a pest to develop resistance to.

The mechanism collapses the moment it gets wet. Dew, rain or irrigation turns
the dust into a harmless paste, and it must be reapplied once the foliage dries.
In a humid climate or under overhead irrigation this makes it close to useless
on leaves, though it remains practical as a dry barrier band around stems or in
a covered position.

Use the horticultural grade. The type sold for swimming-pool filters has been
heat-treated into a form that is a genuine respiratory hazard, and it does not
work any better.

passages.title: Diatomaceous earth and kaolin clay — the mineral dusts — It does not know what it is killing
passages.text:
Any insect that crawls through it is abraded, including ground beetles and other
predators that patrol the soil surface, and it is harmful to bees if applied to
flowers. Band it where the pest travels rather than broadcasting it over
everything, and keep it off blossom.

Wear a dust mask when applying. Fine silica dust is unpleasant to inhale
regardless of grade.

passages.title: Diatomaceous earth and kaolin clay — the mineral dusts — Kaolin clay works by disguise
passages.text:
Kaolin is a fine white clay sprayed as a slurry that dries to a powdery film
over the whole plant. It does not poison anything. It deters insects by making
the surface unrecognisable and physically awkward: the pest cannot identify the
plant as a host, cannot get a grip, and is irritated by particles sticking to it.

Because it is a film, it needs full coverage to work and needs renewing after
heavy rain and as new growth expands unprotected. A partial coat gives the pest
a clean landing site.

Kaolin also reflects sunlight, which reduces heat stress and sunburn on exposed
fruit — often a bigger benefit than the pest control on hot-climate crops.

passages.title: Diatomaceous earth and kaolin clay — the mineral dusts — Where the film is a problem
passages.text:
The white residue is visible at harvest and has to be washed off produce sold
fresh, which can rule it out on a crop sold on appearance close to picking. It
can also interfere with the natural enemies that hunt by sight on the plant
surface, and heavy films can slightly reduce photosynthesis.

Neither dust is a rescue treatment. Both are preventive: they work when they are
already in place before the pest arrives, and they do very little once a
population is established. Always follow the product label and the rules of your
certification body.

passages.title: Neem oil — what it does, and why it is slow — What the active ingredient actually does
passages.text:
Neem's main insecticidal compound is azadirachtin, extracted from the seed of
the neem tree. It is not a contact poison in the way most people expect. It
works mainly as an insect growth regulator and an antifeedant: treated insects
stop feeding, and immature ones fail to moult properly into their next stage.

That mechanism explains the single most common complaint about neem, which is
that "nothing happened". Nothing visibly happens for days. The insects are still
on the plant, and they are still alive, but they have stopped eating and will
not reach adulthood. Judging neem by the count of bodies the next morning will
always make it look like a failure.

passages.title: Neem oil — what it does, and why it is slow — Why it works better on the young
passages.text:
Because the effect runs through moulting, neem hits nymphs and small larvae far
harder than adults. An adult beetle that has finished growing has no moult left
to disrupt, so it may feed less but will not die of it.

The practical consequence is that neem is a tool for early infestations. Once a
population is dominated by adults, neem is close to the wrong choice, and
waiting until damage is obvious usually guarantees that is the population you
have.

passages.title: Neem oil — what it does, and why it is slow — Coverage is the whole game
passages.text:
Azadirachtin does not move through the plant to any useful degree and it breaks
down quickly in sunlight, so it only affects insects it actually lands on or
that eat treated tissue soon after. Aphids on the underside of a leaf are not
touched by a spray that only wetted the top.

This is why neem so often fails on sucking pests sheltering in curled leaves or
growing tips: the spray physically cannot reach them. If the pest is in a place
you cannot wet, neem is not the answer, whatever the label says.

passages.title: Neem oil — what it does, and why it is slow — Effects on other insects
passages.text:
Neem is gentler than the broad-spectrum organic insecticides, but it is not
selective. It can harm predatory larvae and immature parasitic wasps, which are
also growing insects with moults to disrupt. It is toxic to bees while the spray
is still wet, though much less so once dry.

Spraying at dusk, when bees are not flying and the sun will not degrade it
immediately, addresses both the pollinator risk and the breakdown problem at
once. Always follow the product label and the rules of your certification body.

passages.title: Insecticidal soap and horticultural oils — physical, not chemical — How they kill
passages.text:
Insecticidal soaps are potassium salts of fatty acids. They work physically:
the soap disrupts the waxy outer layer of a soft-bodied insect, which then
loses water and collapses. Horticultural oils work by a related physical route,
coating the insect and blocking the spiracles it breathes through.

Neither is a nerve poison and neither leaves a meaningful residue. That has one
enormous consequence for how they are used: **they only work while wet.** Once
the spray has dried, it has no further effect at all, and an insect landing on
the plant an hour later is completely unaffected.

passages.title: Insecticidal soap and horticultural oils — physical, not chemical — Why coverage decides everything
passages.text:
Because the mechanism is contact and momentary, the spray must physically touch
the insect. Not the leaf near the insect — the insect. Aphids on the underside
of a leaf, in a curled tip, or inside a whorl are simply not treated by a spray
directed at the canopy from above.

In practice this means turning leaves over, spraying from beneath where possible,
and accepting that a single pass will never reach everything. It also means these
products fail predictably against anything armoured, mobile, or sheltered, and
succeed against soft, slow, exposed pests like aphids on an open leaf.

passages.title: Insecticidal soap and horticultural oils — physical, not chemical — They are gentle afterwards and harsh at the moment
passages.text:
Having no residue makes soaps and oils among the safest options for beneficial
insects *over time* — a predatory wasp arriving the next day meets nothing. But
at the moment of spraying they are entirely indiscriminate. Any soft-bodied
beneficial that is wetted dies exactly as the aphid does, including ladybird
larvae and hoverfly larvae, which are usually the most valuable things in an
aphid-infested crop.

Spraying only the infested patch, rather than the whole block, preserves the
predator population that will do the rest of the work.

passages.title: Insecticidal soap and horticultural oils — physical, not chemical — Where they damage the crop
passages.text:
Soaps and oils can burn foliage, and the risk rises with heat, bright sun,
drought stress and certain sensitive species. The same physical action that
strips an insect's cuticle can strip a leaf's protective waxes.

Spraying in the cool of early morning or evening, on plants that are not
water-stressed, avoids most of this. Testing on a few plants and waiting a couple
of days before treating a whole block is worth the delay on any crop or variety
you have not sprayed before. Oils must not be combined with sulphur, and the two
should be well separated in time. Always follow the product label and the rules
of your certification body.

passages.title: Spinosad and pyrethrum — the two that need the most care — Spinosad, and why timing protects bees
passages.text:
Spinosad is produced by fermentation of a soil bacterium and acts on the insect
nervous system, by both contact and ingestion. It is genuinely effective against
caterpillars, thrips and several beetles, and it is more persistent than soap or
Bt.

It is also **highly toxic to bees while the spray is wet**, and considerably less
so once it has dried. That single fact drives the standard advice to apply it at
dusk, after foraging has stopped, so the residue is dry before bees return. This
is not a formality; spinosad applied to a flowering crop in the middle of a sunny
morning kills pollinators.

It is toxic to many predatory and parasitic insects too, so it is a tool for a
real infestation rather than a routine one.

passages.title: Spinosad and pyrethrum — the two that need the most care — Spinosad and resistance
passages.text:
Spinosad has a single mode of action, and populations of some pests have already
developed resistance to it where it was used repeatedly as the only control.
Because organic growers have few alternatives, losing spinosad to resistance is
a serious and permanent cost.

Use it sparingly, never on consecutive generations of the same pest, and always
alongside non-chemical controls rather than in place of them.

passages.title: Spinosad and pyrethrum — the two that need the most care — Pyrethrum is fast, broad and blunt
passages.text:
Pyrethrum is extracted from chrysanthemum flowers and attacks the insect nervous
system on contact. It is very fast — insects drop within minutes — and it breaks
down rapidly in sunlight, so it leaves little residue.

Its problem is that it is almost completely non-selective. It kills ladybirds,
lacewings, hoverflies, predatory bugs, parasitic wasps and bees as readily as the
target pest, and because it knocks down the visible adults it can look like a
great success while removing the natural control that was holding the population
down. Rebound infestations after pyrethrum are common and well documented.

It is also highly toxic to fish and other aquatic life, so it must be kept away
from ditches, ponds and watercourses.

passages.title: Spinosad and pyrethrum — the two that need the most care — When pyrethrum is the right call
passages.text:
Rarely, and specifically: a severe infestation, on a crop with real value at
stake, where the alternatives have failed or the pest is not susceptible to
them, and where the block is not flowering. Treat it as an emergency measure
whose cost is the beneficial population, and plan for what happens after.

Note that some pyrethrum products are formulated with piperonyl butoxide, a
synergist that is not permitted under many organic standards. Always check the
product against your own certification body's rules, and follow the label.

passages.title: Integrated pest management — the order to try things in — Why the order matters more than the method
passages.text:
Integrated pest management is not a list of approved products. It is an order of
operations, and the order is what does most of the work. Prevention first, then
monitoring, then physical and biological controls, and only then anything
sprayed — even something organically approved.

Farmers who reverse this end up spraying more, not less, because a spray treats
the insects present today and does nothing about the conditions that brought
them. A field with no flowering margin, continuous host crops and no rotation
will refill with the same pest within a fortnight, and the second outbreak is
usually worse than the first because the natural enemies were sprayed too.

passages.title: Integrated pest management — the order to try things in — Prevention is a planting decision
passages.text:
Most of what determines pest pressure happens before anything is in the ground:
what was grown in that field last year, whether the residue was worked in,
whether the variety has any resistance, when it was sown relative to the pest's
emergence, and how much habitat exists nearby for the predators that would
otherwise do the work for free.

Sowing date is the most underrated of these. Many pests have a narrow window
when they move onto a crop, and a planting shifted by two or three weeks can
miss it entirely. This costs nothing and is invisible in a spray record, which
is precisely why it gets overlooked.

passages.title: Integrated pest management — the order to try things in — Monitoring turns a guess into a decision
passages.text:
Walking the crop on a schedule, looking in the same way each time, is what
separates a decision from a reaction. It tells you whether numbers are rising
or falling, which matters far more than the count on any single day, and it
catches an infestation while it is still confined to one corner.

It also tells you when *not* to act. A great deal of unnecessary spraying is
done against populations that were already collapsing under their own natural
enemies, and the spray then removes those enemies and guarantees a rebound.

passages.title: Integrated pest management — the order to try things in — An organic spray is still a disruption
passages.text:
Approved-for-organic does not mean harmless. Several organic insecticides are
broad-spectrum: they kill predatory beetles, parasitic wasps and pollinators
along with the target. Treat any spray as a last resort with a real cost, not as
the natural end point of noticing a pest.

passages.title: Reading the damage when you cannot find the insect — The damage names the mouthparts
passages.text:
Most of the time the insect has gone and only the damage remains, and the damage
narrows the field considerably because it reflects how the animal eats.

Chewing insects remove tissue: ragged holes, notched leaf edges, whole leaves
stripped to the midrib, or a seedling cut clean through at the base. Caterpillars
and beetle larvae leave holes with irregular edges; adult beetles often leave
small round shot-holes or neat scallops from the margin inward.

Sucking insects remove sap and leave the leaf intact but damaged: pale stippling
or fine speckling, yellowing, curling and distortion of new growth, and sticky
honeydew that later blackens with sooty mould. If a leaf is misshapen but has no
holes in it, stop looking for a caterpillar.

Boring insects leave a small entry hole, often with sawdust-like frass at it, and
a wilting or broken stem above.

passages.title: Reading the damage when you cannot find the insect — Where on the plant, and how old
passages.text:
Damage concentrated on the newest growth points to something feeding on soft
tissue, often a sucking pest sheltering in the tips. Damage on old lower leaves
usually means something working up from the soil. Damage at soil level on a
seedling that has toppled means a cutworm or similar.

Age matters too. Old damage has dried, browned and hardened edges and may have
expanded as the leaf grew; fresh damage is moist and pale at the cut. A field
full of old damage and no new damage needs no treatment at all — a fact that
prevents a great many pointless sprays.

passages.title: Reading the damage when you cannot find the insect — Things that are not insects
passages.text:
A large share of suspected pest damage is not pest damage. Nutrient deficiency
produces yellowing in characteristic patterns, usually symmetrical and without
any tissue removed. Drought and heat scorch leaf margins. Wind abrades and tears.
Herbicide drift distorts new growth in a way that closely mimics sucking-pest
damage. Fungal and bacterial disease produces spots with defined margins, halos
or visible growth.

The distinguishing question is usually whether tissue has been physically
removed. If nothing has been eaten, an insecticide has nothing to do.

passages.title: Reading the damage when you cannot find the insect — When to go and look at night
passages.text:
If leaves are being visibly eaten and daytime searching finds nothing, the
feeder is almost certainly nocturnal. Cutworms, many caterpillars and several
beetles feed after dark and shelter in the soil, under debris or in leaf litter
by morning.

Going out with a torch after dark, or searching the top few centimetres of soil
around a damaged plant, resolves this far more often than any amount of daytime
inspection.

passages.title: Scouting a crop, and deciding whether the damage is worth treating — How to walk a field
passages.text:
Walk a pattern, not the edges. A W or an X across the block, stopping at fixed
points, samples the middle of the crop where problems are usually found later
and are usually worse by then. Edges mislead in both directions: pests that
migrate in are concentrated there, and pests that emerge from the soil are not.

Look at the same number of plants at each stop, and look at the same parts of
each plant — undersides of leaves, growing tips, the stem at soil level, and the
soil itself around the base. Most pests spend most of their time somewhere a
casual glance does not reach, which is why the first sighting is so often the
damage rather than the animal.

Go at the right time of day. Many chewing pests feed at night and shelter in the
soil or leaf litter by mid-morning, so a field that looks clean at noon can be
busy at dusk.

passages.title: Scouting a crop, and deciding whether the damage is worth treating — Counting beats impressions
passages.text:
Write down what you find, at each stop, on each date. The number itself matters
less than the direction it moves. Ten aphids per plant falling is a different
situation from three per plant rising, and no single visit can tell them apart.

Records also let you compare years, which is how you learn whether a rotation or
a habitat planting is actually working on your own ground rather than in theory.

passages.title: Scouting a crop, and deciding whether the damage is worth treating — What an economic threshold is
passages.text:
A threshold is the pest level at which the expected crop loss exceeds the cost
of doing something about it. Below it, treating loses money — the damage would
have cost less than the intervention.

Thresholds are specific to the crop, the growth stage, the market and the
season, and published ones come from particular regions and production systems.
Use them as a way of thinking rather than as numbers to copy: a young transplant
can be killed outright by damage a mature plant would shrug off, and a crop sold
on appearance tolerates far less than one sold for processing.

passages.title: Scouting a crop, and deciding whether the damage is worth treating — Damage is not the same as loss
passages.text:
A plant with chewed outer leaves may yield exactly as much as an untouched one.
Many crops compensate for early leaf loss by growing more leaf, and cosmetic
damage on parts nobody eats or sells costs nothing at all.

Ask what is actually being lost before treating: the growing point, the harvested
organ, the plant's ability to stand up, or only the appearance of a leaf that
will be discarded anyway.
